about.title: Placerville Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Placerville residents rely on a mix of local clinics and larger El Dorado County medical facilities for care, and most visits go as expected. But when a provider misses a diagnosis, makes a surgical error, or mishandles medication, the consequences can be lasting. California treats these cases differently than a typical injury claim — there's a shorter window to act, a required notice period before filing suit, and rules about what a case must show to move forward. If you believe a medical error caused you harm in Placerville, it helps to understand your situation early rather than wait. We handle medical malpractice claims directly and can review what happened and explain your options under California's malpractice framework. There's no obligation, and if we take your case forward, we work on contingency — meaning no fee unless you recover.

whyChoose.title: Why Understanding California's Malpractice Rules Matters

items.title: Strict, Layered Deadlines
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from when you discover the harm, but never more than three years from the injury itself, to bring a claim. Missing either deadline can end a case before it starts.

items.title: Mandatory 90-Day Notice
items.desc: Before filing suit, California law requires sending the provider a 90-day notice of intent. Our team handles this process carefully to make sure it's done correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Is Usually Required
items.desc: A bad medical outcome by itself isn't enough — California generally requires a qualified medical expert to support the claim that the standard of care was breached. We help get that process moving right away.

items.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim in Placerville?
items.answer: Under California's MICRA rules, you generally have one year from when you discover the injury, but no more than three years from the date it occurred, whichever comes first. These deadlines are strict, so it's worth having your situation reviewed as soon as possible.

items.question: Is a bad medical outcome automatically malpractice?
items.answer: No. California law requires showing that a provider's care fell below an accepted medical standard, not just that the result was disappointing or unexpected. This is typically established through a qualified medical expert's review of your records.

items.question: Are there limits on what I can recover in a California malpractice case?
items.answer: California caps non-economic damages, like pain and suffering, though that cap rises each year under current law. Economic damages, such as medical bills and lost income, are generally not subject to that same cap. Our team can walk you through how this applies to your specific circumstances.
